title: Case studies: the Amazon and the Namib

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Case studies of an area of tropical rainforest, the Amazon in Brazil, and an area of hot desert, the Namib of Namibia: their character, the ways people use them, and the challenges each sets.

blocks.heading: Case study: the Amazon rainforest, Brazil
blocks.text: The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest area of tropical rainforest on Earth, covering about 5.5 million square kilometres, of which about 60 per cent lies inside Brazil. Its climate is equatorial, hot and wet in every month, and its rivers carry a vast share of the world's fresh water to the sea. For a place-specific focus, take the state of Rondonia in western Brazil, a famous deforestation frontier. The BR-364 highway, paved in the 1980s, opened the forest to settlement: migrants cleared plots for small farms, and loggers, cattle ranches and later soya farms followed the road inland. Cattle ranching is the leading use of the land after clearing, and herds graze pastures that were rainforest a generation ago. Brazil protects parts of the Amazon with national parks and indigenous reserves, and its satellite monitoring publishes clearing figures each year: about 28 000 square kilometres cleared in 2004, about 4 600 in 2012, and about 13 000 by 2021. The detail worth remembering is Rondonia, the BR-364, cattle and soya on the cleared land, and the swing of the satellite figures. The forest's own character explains why the loss matters: the canopy holds so much moisture that a cleared plot dries hard within a few years, the thin soil exhausts after two or three harvests, and the farmers move on to clear again, so the frontier advances rather than settles. The rainforest's structure, layer on layer from emergent trees through closed canopy to the dark floor, is what the chainsaws remove, and with it the plants, the insects and the birds that no other ground can replace.

blocks.heading: Case study: the Namib Desert
blocks.text: The Namib runs along the Atlantic coast of southern Angola, Namibia and the Northern Cape of South Africa for about 2000 kilometres, and it is counted among the oldest deserts on Earth. Rainfall near the coast is usually under 20 millimetres a year, but fog drifting inland over the cold Benguela Current dampens the coast on up to 180 days a year, and much of the desert's life depends on that fog. The welwitschia, a plant with two ragged ribbon-like leaves that lives for over a thousand years, drinks moisture from the air; oryx and other antelope graze the sparse grass at dawn and dusk. People cluster where water can be found. Topnaar communities herd goats along the dry Kuiseb valley and gather the nara melon, and boreholes supply homesteads far from any river. The desert is also a working landscape: the open-pit uranium mine at Rossing, near Arandis inland of Walvis Bay, has operated since 1976, its mine and town drawing water from underground, and tourism is the second pillar, centred on the red dunes above 300 metres at Sossusvlei in the Namib-Naukluft area. Along the coast, Swakopmund and Walvis Bay sit where the desert meets the cold ocean, and their moored fishing fleet, salt works and tour operators all live off the desert's edge: the fog cools the towns, the dunes bring the visitors, and the cold current feeds the fish. The two case studies of this unit answer any 7-mark question that names an area of tropical rainforest or an area of hot desert, and they pair as opposites: one ecosystem drowning in rain it cannot store, the other drinking fog because rain almost never comes, and the same syllabus skills, structure, adaptation, human use and threat, answer for both.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The Namib connects to topic 2.4's weather, which explains fog over cold water, and to topic 2.2's rivers, where the Kuiseb appears as an ephemeral river; the Amazon links to topic 3.7's environmental risks and to topic 3.2's farming, since cleared forest often becomes farmland. Topic 4's skills work uses both case studies' maps.
